{{Short description|Fluid motion of gaseous detonation products}}
'''Zeldovich–Taylor flow''' (also known as '''Zeldovich–Taylor expansion wave''') is the fluid motion of gaseous detonation products behind [[Chapman–Jouguet condition|Chapman–Jouguet]] [[detonation wave]]. The flow was described independently by [[Yakov Zeldovich]] in 1942<ref>Zeldovich, Y. B. (1942). On the distribution of pressure and velocity in the products of a detonation explosion, specifically in the case of spherical propagation of the detonation wave. Journal Experimental Theoretical Physics, 12(1), 389.</ref><ref>Zeldovich, Y. B., & Kompaneets, Alexander Solomonovich (1960). Theory of detonation. Academic Press, Section 23, pp. 279-284</ref> and [[G. I. Taylor]] in 1950,<ref>Taylor, G. I. (1950). The dynamics of the combustion products behind plane and spherical detonation fronts in explosives. Proceedings of the Royal Society of London. Series A. Mathematical and Physical Sciences, 200(1061), 235-247.</ref> although [[G. I. Taylor]] carried out the work in 1941 that being circulated in the British Ministry of Home Security. Since naturally occurring detonation waves are in general a [[Chapman–Jouguet condition|Chapman–Jouguet]] [[detonation wave]], the solution becomes very useful in describing real-life detonation waves.

==Mathematical description==
Consider a spherically outgoing [[Chapman–Jouguet condition|Chapman–Jouguet]] [[detonation wave]] propagating with a constant velocity <math>D</math>. By definition, immediately behind the detonation wave, the gas velocity is equal to the local [[sound speed]] <math>c</math> with respect to the wave. Let <math>v(r,t)</math> be the [[radial velocity]] of the gas behind the wave, in a fixed frame. The detonation is ignited at <math>t=0</math> at <math>r=0</math>. For <math>t>0</math>, the gas velocity must be zero at the center <math>r=0</math> and should take the value <math>v=D-c</math> at the detonation location <math>r = Dt</math>. The fluid motion is governed by the inviscid [[Euler equations (fluid dynamics)|Euler equations]]<ref>Sedov, L. I., & Volkovets, A. G. (2018). Similarity and dimensional methods in mechanics. CRC press.</ref>

<math display="block">
\begin{align}
\frac{\partial \rho}{\partial t} + v\frac{\partial \rho}{\partial r} &= - \rho\left(\frac{\partial v}{\partial r} + \frac{2v}{r}\right),\\
\frac{\partial v}{\partial t} + v \frac{\partial v}{\partial r} &= - \frac{1}{\rho}\frac{\partial p}{\partial r},\\
\frac{\partial s}{\partial t} + v \frac{\partial s}{\partial r} &= 0
\end{align}
</math>
where <math>\rho</math> is the density, <math>p</math> is the pressure and <math>s</math> is the entropy. The last equation implies that the flow is isentropic and hence we can write <math>c^2 = dp/d\rho</math>.

Since there are no length or time scales involved in the problem, one may look for a [[self-similar solution]] of the form {{nowrap|<math>v(r,t)=v(\xi)</math>,}} {{nowrap|<math>p(r,t) = p(\xi)</math>,}} {{nowrap|<math>\rho(r,t) = \rho(\xi)</math>}}, {{nowrap|<math>c(r,t) = c(\xi)</math>,}} where {{nowrap|<math>\xi = r/t</math>.}} The first two equations then become

<math display="block">
\begin{align}
(\xi-v)\rho'/\rho &= v' + 2v/\xi,\\
(\xi-v) v' &= p'/\rho = c^2 \rho'/\rho
\end{align}
</math>
where prime denotes differentiation with respect to <math>\xi</math>. We can eliminate <math>\rho'/\rho</math> between the two equations to obtain an equation that contains only <math>v</math> and <math>c</math>. Because of the isentropic condition, we can express <math>\rho = \rho(c), \, p=p(c)</math>, that is to say, we can replace <math>\rho^{-1}d\rho/dx</math> with <math>\rho^{-1}c'd\rho/dc</math>. This leads to

<math display="block">\begin{align}
(\xi-v)\frac{1}{\rho}\frac{d\rho}{dc} c' &= v' + \frac{2v}{\xi},\\
\left[\frac{(\xi-v)^2}{c^2}-1\right]v' &= \frac{2v}{\xi}.
\end{align}
</math>

For [[polytropic gas]]es with constant specific heats, we have <math>\rho^{-1}d\rho/dc = 2/[(\gamma-1)c]</math>. The above set of equations cannot be solved analytically, but has to be integrated numerically. The solution has to be found for the range <math>0\leq \xi \leq D</math> subjected to the condition <math>\xi-v=c</math> at <math>\xi=D.</math> 

The function <math>v(\xi)</math> is found to monotonically decrease from its value <math>v(D) = c(D)-D</math> to zero at a finite value of <math>\xi<D</math>, where a weak discontinuity (that is a function is continuous, but its derivatives may not) exists. The region between the detonation front and the trailing weak discontinuity is the [[rarefaction]] (or expansion) flow. Interior to the weak discontinuity <math>v=0</math> everywhere.

===Location of the weak discontinuity ([[Mach wave]])===
From the second equation described above, it follows that when <math>v=0</math>, <math>\xi=c</math>. More precisely, as <math>v\rightarrow 0</math>, that equation can be approximated as<ref>Landau, L. D., & Lifshitz, E. M. (1987). Fluid Mechanics Pergamon. New York, section 130, pp-496-499.</ref>

<math display="block">(\ln v)' = 2c^2/[\xi(\xi^2-c^2)].</math>

As <math>v \to 0</math>, <math>\ln v \to -\infty</math> and <math>(\ln v)' \to \infty</math> if <math>\xi</math> decreases as <math>v \to 0</math>. The left hand side of the above equation can become positive infinity only if <math>\xi \to c</math>. Thus, when <math>\xi</math> decreases to the value <math>\xi = c_0</math>, the gas comes to rest (Here <math>c_0</math> is the sound speed corresponding to <math>v=0</math>). Thus, the rarefaction motion occurs for <math>c_0<\xi\leq D</math> and there is no fluid motion for <math>0\leq \xi \leq c_0</math>.

===Behavior near the weak discontinuity===
Rewrite the second equation as

<math display="block">v\frac{d\xi}{dv} = \frac{1}{2}\xi\left[\frac{(\xi-v)^2}{c^2}-1\right].</math>

In the neighborhood of the weak discontinuity, the quantities to the first order (such as <math>v,\,\xi-c_0,\,c-c_0</math>) reduces the above equation to

<math display="block">v\frac{d}{dv}(\xi-c_0) = (\xi-c_0) - (v+c-c_0).</math>

At this point, it is worth mentioning that in general, disturbances in gases are propagated with respect to the gas at the local sound speed. In other words, in the fixed frame, the disturbances are propagated at the speed <math>v+c</math> (the other possibility is <math>v-c</math> although it is of no interest here). If the gas is at rest <math>v=0</math>, then the disturbance speed is <math>c_0</math>. This is just a normal sound wave propagation. If however <math>v</math> is non-zero but a small quantity, then one find the correction for the disturbance propagation speed as <math>v+c=c_0 + \alpha_0 v</math> obtained using a [[Taylor series]] expansion, where <math>\alpha_0</math> is the [[Landau derivative]] (for [[ideal gas]], <math>\alpha_0 = (\gamma+1)/2</math>, where <math>\gamma</math> is the [[specific heat ratio]]). This means that the above equation can be written as

<math display="block">v\frac{d}{dv}(\xi-c_0) - (\xi-c_0) = \alpha_0 v</math>

whose solution is

<math display="block">\xi-c_0 = \alpha_0 v\ln (A/v)</math>

where <math>A</math> is a constant. This determines <math>v(\xi)</math> implicitly in the neighborhood of the week discontinuity where <math>v</math> is small. This equation shows that at <math>\xi=c_0</math>, <math>v=0</math>, <math>dv/d\xi=0</math>, but all higher-order derivatives are discontinuous. In the above equation, subtract <math>v+c-c_0</math> from the left-hand side and <math>\alpha_0v</math> from the right-hand side to obtain

<math display="block">\xi-v-c = (\xi-c_0)-(v+c-c_0)=\alpha_0 v[\ln(A/v)-1]</math>

which implies that <math>\xi-v>c</math> if <math>v</math> is a small quantity. It can be shown that the relation <math>\xi-v>c</math> not only holds for small <math>v</math>, but throughout the rarefaction wave. 

===Behavior near the detonation front===
First let us show that the relation <math>\xi-v>c</math> is not only valid near the weak discontinuity, but throughout the region. If this inequality is not maintained, then there must be a point where <math>\xi-v=c,\, v\neq 0</math> between the weak discontinuity and the detonation front. The second governing equation implies that at this point <math>v'</math> must be infinite or, <math>d\xi/dv=0</math>. Let us obtain <math>d^2\xi/dv^2</math> by taking the [[second derivative]] of the governing equation. In the resulting equation, impose the condition <math>\xi-v=c,\,v\neq 0,\, d\xi/dv=0</math> to obtain <math>d^2\xi/dv^2 = -\alpha_0 \xi/c_0v\neq 0</math>. This implies that <math>\xi(v)</math> reaches a maximum at this point which in turn implies that <math>v(\xi)</math> cannot exist for <math>\xi</math> greater than the maximum point considered since otherwise <math>v(\xi)</math> would be multi-valued. The maximum point at most can be corresponded to the outer boundary (detonation front). This means that <math>\xi-v-c</math> can vanish only on the boundary and it is already shown that <math>\xi-v-c</math> is positive near the weak discontinuity, <math>\xi-v-c</math> is positive everywhere in the region except the boundaries where it can vanish. 

Note that near the detonation front, we must satisfy the condition <math>\xi-v=c,\, v\neq 0</math>. The value evaluated at <math>\xi=D</math> for the function <math>\xi-v</math>, i.e., <math>D-v(D)</math> is nothing but the velocity of the detonation front with respect to the gas velocity behind it. For a detonation front, the condition <math>D-v(D)\leq c(D)</math> must always be met, with the equality sign representing Chapman–Jouguet detonations and the inequalities representing over-driven detonations. The analysis describing the point <math>\xi-v=c,\, v\neq 0</math> must correspond to the detonation front.
